analysis.one_liner: Sets a regional minimum wage at half the local cost of living and raises the tipped worker wage floor.
analysis.headline: The Fair Wage Act was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on December 12, 2023, and received no hearing, vote, or further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the flat $7.25 federal minimum wage with a regional wage tied to local prices: each metro area's minimum would start at 40% of the national average private-sector hourly wage and rise to 50% within two years, adjusting upward every three years. It would also raise the separate, lower cash wage employers must pay tipped workers, and change the rules for teenage new hires. It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, minimum-wage workers would gain the most: the federal floor would roughly double in most areas, phased in over two years, with the largest gains in expensive metros like New York and San Francisco. Tipped workers would gain a cash wage floor ten times the current $2.13. Employers paying above the minimum would face competitive pressure to keep pay ahead.

how_it_helps.text: It sets the federal minimum wage in each metro area at 40% of the national average private-sector hourly wage, rising to 45% after a year and 50% after two years — roughly $12 to $15 an hour depending on the area.
It raises the floor again every three years, so the minimum can never fall behind rising pay in high-wage regions.
It cuts the tipped cash wage floor from $2.13 to 30% of the local minimum, narrowing a gap that has stood since 1991.
It adjusts for regional prices, so the wage is set to local living costs rather than a single national number.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum wage — restaurants, retail, care work, agriculture — would bear the cost of roughly doubling the wage floor, likely passed on in prices, reduced hours, or automation. Tipped-restaurant owners would additionally lose the $2.13 tipped credit.

drawbacks.text: Because the wage is set regionally, the raise is smaller in low-cost areas: the same 40-50% of average pay applies everywhere, so a worker in a cheap metro gets a lower wage floor than one in an expensive one.

Employers paying the minimum wage would face phased increases starting within three months of enactment, a cost small businesses and franchise operators consistently argue leads to reduced hiring or hours.
Tipped workers would still earn a subminimum cash wage — 30% of the local minimum — rather than the full minimum before tips, so their guaranteed pay stays low and depends on customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's design is a deliberate trade-off: tying the minimum wage to local living costs avoids abrupt hikes in low-cost regions, which reduces job-loss risk but also means workers in cheap areas get a smaller raise. The main cost falls on employers who pay minimum wage, especially in high-cost metros. The biggest drawback is not in the design but in the fate: it never received a hearing or a vote, so its benefits were never weighed on the record at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there, with no hearing, vote, or further action, until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The House referred the bill to the Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, December 12, 2023.
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended; minimum wage bills not reported out of committee in that Congress received no floor consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum wage, including restaurant and retail chains, are better off because no higher wage floor ever took effect. Workers earning $7.25 an hour gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee on December 12, 2023.

for.name: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action or a floor vote; with the chamber's agenda controlled by the majority, a wage increase bill from the Education and Workforce Committee's docket had no path forward.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, a bipartisan pairing, but with only two members behind it there was never enough support to test where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill both raises the minimum they must pay and narrows the tipped subminimum wage to 30% of the local minimum, directly increasing labor costs in an industry that is a heavy user of both minimum-wage and tipped workers.
Any employer paying near the current $7.25 minimum would face a wage floor roughly 70-100% higher, phased in over two years. Workers and their communities gain the difference.
